prompt.raw:
[{"content":"You are extracting a teacher's spoken notes about the children in one class.

The notes arrive as a transcript, in the order the teacher spoke them. The children in this
class are listed below. Names in the transcript are speech-to-text and often misspelt or
mangled; match a spoken name to the listed child it most plausibly is.

Return "observations": the transcript cut into contiguous passages, in order, one passage
per owner, together covering the whole transcript.

Each passage has:
- "kind":
  - "child" — the teacher is talking about one individual child and speaks a name for them.
  - "absent" — the teacher says a named child was not there today ("Théo wasn't in today").
  - "unknown" — the teacher is talking about one individual child but no name is spoken for
    them in this passage or the passage it continues: only a pronoun. Do not guess. The
    teacher will assign it.
  - "group" — a statement about the class as a whole, using a collective referent
    ("everyone", "all the kids", "the class", "they" meaning the whole group). A statement
    that names one child, or describes only one child, is NEVER "group", however it is
    joined to the rest of the sentence.
  - "none" — not an observation about children: the class header, a greeting,
    vocabulary the children are being taught, thinking aloud that describes no child and
    no class.
- "spoken_labels": for a "child" or "absent" passage, the name the teacher speaks for it,
  verbatim as spoken, uncorrected. Empty list for "unknown", "group" and "none".
- "student": for a "child" or "absent" passage, the listed child's name exactly as listed
  below, or "" when no listed child fits. "" for every other kind.
- "summary": the observations in that passage, rewritten as clear sentences.

Rules:
- A child passage runs from where the teacher starts talking about that child to where the
  teacher moves on. It usually opens with the child's name and then continues in pronouns;
  every pronoun sentence after that name belongs to that child until the next child is
  named. Do NOT open a new passage for a pronoun the teacher is still using for the same
  child.
- When the teacher makes the same observation about several named children at once
  ("Zachariah and Anaya did very well", "they both worked well"), return that passage once
  PER CHILD: the same summary repeated, each copy with its own "student". Never fold two
  named children into one passage. This holds when the shared remark opens its own sentence
  after the names: each copy's "spoken_labels" holds the name the teacher spoke for that
  child, never "they" or "both". The shared passage runs from the names to where the teacher
  moves on, pronoun sentences included: after "Maya and Noor did well", a "They did well with
  the colours" belongs to both, so every copy carries the whole of it. The copies differ only
  in "student" and "spoken_labels"; a copy shorter than another is wrong. If the
  observations differ between the children, they are separate passages with different
  summaries. A statement about the class as a whole is still one "group" passage, not one
  per child.
- "student" is set ONLY when the passage's own words, or the passage it continues, speak
  a name for the child — a name that appears in "spoken_labels". A passage that refers to
  the child only by a pronoun ("she", "he") has NO student: it is "unknown", even when
  exactly one listed child has not been mentioned yet. Children on the list who are never
  named were not discussed today. Never assign a passage to a child by
  elimination, by roster order, or because they are the only one left.
- The list of children exists to spell spoken names correctly, not to decide who is
  present.
- The summary uses ONLY the words in its own passage. Never bring in an observation from
  another passage, even an adjacent one.
- The summary keeps the teacher's voice: their vocabulary, their tone, first person if they
  used it. Clean up false starts, filler words and repetitions. Do NOT soften, formalise,
  add or editorialise.
- "none" never takes an observation with it. The header passage ends with the header
  itself: the first sentence that describes the children opens a new passage, even when it
  is spoken in the same breath.

The children in this class:
- Emma
- Ryan
- Lila
","role":"system"},{"content":"Um, so today I wanted to talk about Emma. She, uh, she did great in math today, really got the hang of the multiplication tables we've been working on. And then, let's see... I also wanted to mention Ryan. Ryan was, he was really struggling with the reading comprehension exercise, couldn't quite get the main idea from the passage. Yeah, that's, that's about it for today.","role":"user"}]
prompt.label: gradebee-prompt

students.name: Emma
students.quoted_text: Emma did great in math today, really got the hang of the multiplication tables we've been working on.

students.name: Ryan
students.quoted_text: Ryan was really struggling with the reading comprehension exercise, couldn't quite get the main idea from the passage.

Chloé shows a generally positive attitude toward classroom activities, though her engagement varies. She is willing to participate in group tasks, such as the "Emma is wearing..." activity, and demonstrates cooperation with peers and the teacher. However, she occasionally holds back when new material is introduced, as seen when she repeatedly asked for clarification on tasks she already understood, which required redirection. Her participation improves when working with familiar structures, such as telling her age and gender or repeating story elements, where she contributes more confidently.

BEHAVIOUR

Chloé is integrated within the group but can be easily distracted, particularly when tired or when instructions are being given. She sometimes requires reminders to focus, as noted when she repeatedly asked "quoi quoi quoi" during workshop instructions. Her mood and attentiveness fluctuate; on one occasion, she was in a very good mood and engaged well, while on another, she was noted as distracted and tired. The group’s playful and occasionally loud demeanor sometimes influences her behavior, but she responds well to reminders and calms down when prompted.

Use of structures: Chloé can use basic structures, such as stating her age and gender, often with the complete form. response.output:
Motivation and Participation

Chloé showed interest in a range of classroom activities. She liked the “What’s missing?” activity, was excited to hear more of the new story and enjoyed the story tattoo activity. She was also in a very good mood during one session. When the traffic-light system was introduced after the group had been loud at the beginning, she participated very well. She responded to reminders and stopped repeatedly asking where to place items when asked to do so.

Chloé took part in the activities and practised the language being worked on. She could tell her age and gender, usually using the complete structure, repeat new vocabulary and structures, and take part in the story, worksheet, clothing, body-part and bingo activities. At times, she needed encouragement or support to participate independently, particularly when new vocabulary or instructions were introduced. She sometimes asked for information that she already knew and needed help with vocabulary cards and with telling the story.

Behaviour

Chloé’s attention varied during the sessions. On one occasion, she was distracted and tired, and on another she needed to pay closer attention to the teacher’s workshop instructions. The group was sometimes playful and loud, but it calmed down when reminded, and the traffic-light system helped the children to participate more effectively.

Chloé responded to adult reminders and was able to continue with the activities. During one activity, her repeated questions became frustrating for the teacher and another student, but she stopped when this was explained to her. She also worked alongside the other students in the group activities, sometimes with a little help.

Learning

Chloé demonstrated progress with several of the structures and concepts covered. She could tell her age and gender, almost always using the complete structure, repeat new vocabulary and structures, pair the correct actions with the correct rooms, and understand the clean/dirty and dry/wet concepts. She could pair Emma’s clean and dirty body parts, although she needed a reminder to use the full structure. She also understood the “Emma is wearing…” activity and could repeat the appropriate structure while cleaning and dressing Emma.

Chloé participated successfully in worksheet activities and could count very well. She could place clothing items on and take them off, identify the corresponding colour and clothing item on her bingo card, and place tattoos and stickers on the correct body parts with a little help. She partially understood the Numbers songs.

Further practice is needed with colours and clothes vocabulary. Chloé needed help with vocabulary cards because the teacher had to provide the word and image, and she did not initially know the colours or clothing items. Her understanding of the story varied: on one occasion she needed help to tell it, while on another she knew it very well. Continued classroom practice will focus on recalling the story, consolidating colour and clothing vocabulary, following instructions attentively and using the complete structures more independently.

Objectives and content of the Oliver course, 3rd term

---

Term report (3rd term)

Data

  • Name: Mila
  • Teacher: Thérèse Garnier
  • Level: Oliver · Thu 2025/2026
  • Period: 2026-02-22 to 2026-05-22

Participation/Motivation

Assessment (Participation / Motivation): Good

Comment: Mila generally comes to class in a positive mood and shows interest in the activities presented. She is usually willing to participate and can be very engaged when she feels comfortable with the task, especially in action-based activities and games. At times, however, she can become upset when things do not go as she expects, which affects her willingness to continue taking part. With encouragement, she is able to rejoin the class and show good motivation, particularly when she has the opportunity to help or demonstrate what she knows.

Learning process

Assessment (Learning process): Good

Comment: Mila has shown good understanding of the structures and vocabulary worked on this term. She can repeat the target language well and, in many activities, uses the new language with confidence. Her knowledge of the story has improved notably, and she is able to retell parts of it with little support. She also performs very well in activities involving weather, clothing, and colour vocabulary. At times, she still needs help with some specific words and routines, such as taking off and putting on, and she may need further practice to remain consistent when new language is introduced. Continued repetition and reinforcement will help her consolidate her progress even further.

Behaviour

Assessment (Behaviour): Good

Comment: Mila is well integrated in the group and can participate positively in class. On the whole, she behaves appropriately and works well with the rest of the students, especially during practical and familiar activities. However, when she becomes frustrated or does not get her way, she may withdraw, refuse to participate, or show signs of anger, which can affect her focus during the lesson. She sometimes needs reminders to stay engaged and remain seated during story time. When she is calm, she responds well and shows a much more cooperative attitude.

Marks

Oral Test Mark: 8.00    Good. Mila can understand the question and answers either with a single word or with a structure which is only partially correct.

Final comment

Mila has made good progress this term and has shown that she can understand and use a great deal of the language worked on in class. Her ability to repeat structures, recognise vocabulary, and take part in action activities is very promising. With continued encouragement to manage moments of frustration and to stay engaged throughout the whole lesson, she will be able to keep building confidence and continue developing her English skills successfully.

Motivation and Participation

Mila often comes to class in a happy mood and has shown enjoyment during classroom activities. She was happy to participate in the action activity and enjoyed activities such as A Present for Me, the Dice Game and Family Bingo. She also wanted to help hand out materials. At times, however, she became upset when she could not do an activity in the way she wanted or when she was not allowed to keep a resource. On these occasions, she sometimes initially listened without joining in or refused to take part in particular activities. With support, her participation improved.

Mila participates well when she is engaged in an activity and can use previously learned language. She knew much of the vocabulary, structures, songs, gestures and story, and could repeat and use the language during the activities. She could also tell most of the story with very little help. We will continue to encourage her to join in from the beginning of each activity, especially when a new task or a change of plan is introduced.

Behaviour

Mila is integrated into the class activities and has shown that she can work positively with the group, for example by helping to hand out materials and participating in shared games. Her behaviour was relatively good during one of the lessons, and she responded well during the action and worksheet activities.

When she became upset, Mila sometimes found it difficult to re-engage. She closed up when she did not get her way, refused to join the True or False activity and Dice Game on one occasion, and turned her back during the story when she was angry. She also lay down several times and needed reminders to sit. In another lesson, she said she had a headache before later taking part in the activities. We will continue to support her in expressing her feelings, coping with disappointment and returning calmly to the group.

Learning

Mila has made good progress with the language and story work. She knew most of the vocabulary and structures and understood how to use the structures during activities. She could combine moods and actions very well, match the phrase to her weather card, and use the weather and clothing combinations successfully. She learned to say what she was wearing and demonstrated her understanding of the colour vocabulary, including white and black.

Mila could repeat the target structures very well and could tell part of the story independently, repeating the rest with support. She could also identify who was missing, name the family member, repeat the correct structure, pair sentences with the appropriate weather realia and say most of the words, although she sometimes needed help. She completed the worksheet activity very well and performed the action activity successfully.

She still needs support with the words “taking off” and “putting on”, and sometimes needs help recalling vocabulary. Her participation can also be affected when she is disappointed or upset. We will continue practising these clothing expressions and vocabulary through the weather routines, stories and action activities, while encouraging Mila to remain involved and use the structures even when an activity does not go as she expects.

Motivation and Participation

Motivation: Camille demonstrates a positive attitude toward classroom activities. She shows willingness to learn, as evidenced by her attentiveness and engagement with new stories and routines. She is open to new activities, quickly understanding and participating in the weather and action miming routine, as well as the mood routine. Camille is generally cooperative with the group and the teacher, though she occasionally engages in playful behavior with peers, such as hiding materials jokingly.

Participation: Camille actively participates in classroom activities, particularly those she enjoys, such as "A Present for Me," the Dice Game, and Family Bingo. Behaviour

Camille is generally well-integrated within the group and maintains focus during activities. However, she can be slightly distracting at times, particularly when interacting playfully with peers like Zoé. Her behavior is influenced by her mood; for instance, she was less confident on one occasion but responded well to encouragement.   • Tends to hold back when less confident; encouragement helps her regain focus.

Motivation and Participation

Motivation: Camille demonstrates a positive attitude toward classroom activities. She shows willingness to learn, as evidenced by her attentiveness and engagement with new stories and routines. She is open to new activities, quickly understanding and participating in the weather and action miming routine, as well as the mood routine. Camille is generally cooperative with the group and the teacher, though she occasionally engages in playful behavior with peers, such as hiding materials jokingly.

Participation: Camille actively participates in classroom activities, particularly those she enjoys, such as "A Present for Me," the Dice Game, and Family Bingo. Motivation and Participation

Camille generally comes to activities with a positive attitude and shows enjoyment when learning through stories, games and routines. She really enjoyed the new story, was very happy to listen to it, and particularly loved activities such as “A Present for Me,” “Who’s Missing?”, Family Bingo and the Dice Game. She was attentive overall and showed willingness to repeat when asked. She also quickly understood the new weather and action-miming routine, as well as the mood routine using “he’s smiling because he’s happy.”

Camille participates in classroom activities and demonstrates understanding of the tasks. She understood the worksheet activity about what Oliver and Baby could or could not do, and showed a good understanding and some memorisation of the vocabulary. She could recite parts of the story, although she was sometimes less confident and hesitant. She is still developing her ability to ask questions about a person’s physical appearance before asking who it is.

Behaviour

Camille is often attentive and was described as very attentive during some activities. She was integrated into the group and enjoyed participating with her classmates. At times, she became playful and distracting with Zoé. She also jokingly hid the material and did not always give it back directly when asked. These moments were manageable, and her overall behaviour was considered very positive; the teacher was particularly proud of the group’s behaviour.

Like the rest of the group, Camille became bored towards the end of the story. She was also a little less confident and more hesitant during one session, but responded positively to encouragement and appeared happy.

Learning

Camille is making progress in using the language and structures introduced in class. She could remember vocabulary very well, including colours and clothing items, and could remember some prepositions. She understood the worksheet tasks and could repeat language when prompted. She also quickly understood and used the new weather, action and mood routines.

Camille can recite part of the story and shows real understanding and some memorisation of the vocabulary. However, she often needed help to remember the correct structures during activities, and she is still developing confidence when speaking. Asking questions about physical appearance before identifying someone is also still a work in progress.

To support her progress, we will continue to encourage Camille to speak with confidence, practise the correct structures during activities, and reinforce the question patterns used to describe and identify people. Positive encouragement has already helped her to participate when she feels hesitant.
